# Deterministic Büchi Automata Are Strictly Weaker

For **finite** words, complementing a DFA is a one-line trick: complete it with a sink and swap accepting / non-accepting states. This fails for Büchi automata for two reasons — nondeterminism (no unique run to reverse) and, more deeply, that **deterministic Büchi automata (DBA) recognise strictly fewer languages than nondeterministic ones (NBA)**.

The running witness is the complement of "infinitely many saves". After the initial `open`, over $\Gamma=\{\texttt{edit},\texttt{save},\texttt{idle}\}$:
$$ \overline{L}=\{\alpha : \text{only finitely many } \texttt{save}\text{ occur}\}. $$

This notebook shows both halves of the gap: an NBA **does** recognise $\overline L$, and a natural DBA attempt provably **fails**.

---

## Widget 1: The NBA recognises $\overline{L}$

The NBA **guesses** the position after which no more `save` ever arrives, then jumps to an accepting component that reads only `edit`/`idle` (a `save` there kills the run). A word $u\cdot v^{\omega}$ has only finitely many saves **iff its period $v$ contains no `save`**.

<script>
(function(){
  const parse=s=>s.trim().split(/[\s,]+/).filter(x=>x.length);
  const PRE=[{u:'open',v:'edit idle'},{u:'open',v:'edit save'},{u:'open save save',v:'idle'},{u:'open',v:'save idle'}];
  function run(){
    const u=parse(document.getElementById('nb16-u').value), v=parse(document.getElementById('nb16-v').value);
    const strip=document.getElementById('nb16-strip'), verdict=document.getElementById('nb16-verdict');
    strip.innerHTML=''; verdict.innerHTML='';
    if(!v.length){verdict.innerHTML="<div class='verdict-box verdict-fail'>Period cannot be empty.</div>";return;}
    const seq=u.concat(...Array(3).fill(v));
    seq.forEach((s,i)=>{const d=document.createElement('span');d.className='tok'+(s==='save'?' save':'')+(i<u.length?' stem':'');d.textContent=s;strip.appendChild(d);});
    const savesInPeriod = v.includes('save');
    if(!savesInPeriod){
      verdict.innerHTML=`<div class="verdict-box verdict-pass"><strong>&alpha; &isin; L&#773; — accepted by the NBA.</strong><br>The period has no <code>save</code>, so after the stem no save ever returns. The NBA guesses the split right after the stem and reads the save-free tail in its accepting component. Only finitely many saves occur.</div>`;
    } else {
      verdict.innerHTML=`<div class="verdict-box verdict-fail"><strong>&alpha; &notin; L&#773; — rejected.</strong><br>The period contains <code>save</code>, so saves recur <em>infinitely often</em>. Wherever the NBA guesses the last save, a later save kills that accepting branch. No accepting run exists.</div>`;
    }
  }
  function loadPreset(){const p=PRE[+document.getElementById('nb16-preset').value];document.getElementById('nb16-u').value=p.u;document.getElementById('nb16-v').value=p.v;run();}
  document.getElementById('nb16-preset').addEventListener('change',loadPreset);
  document.getElementById('nb16-run').addEventListener('click',run);
  ['nb16-u','nb16-v'].forEach(id=>document.getElementById(id).addEventListener('keyup',e=>{if(e.key==='Enter')run();}));
  loadPreset();
})();
</script>

---

## Widget 2: Any deterministic attempt fails

Here is the most natural DBA one might try for $\overline L$ — call it $\mathcal D$. It accepts whenever it keeps seeing non-`save` symbols:

- $d_0$ (**accepting**): reading `edit` or `idle` stays / returns here.
- $d_1$ (non-accepting): reading `save` goes here.

$\mathcal D$ visits its accepting state $d_0$ infinitely often exactly when `edit`/`idle` occur infinitely often — which is **not** the same as "finitely many saves". The button below feeds $\mathcal D$ the adversarial word $(\texttt{save}\ \texttt{idle})^{\omega}$: it has **infinitely many saves** (so it is *not* in $\overline L$), yet $\mathcal D$ accepts it.

```{=html}
<div class="sc-lab" id="nb16b">
  <div class="input-row" style="align-items:center;">
    <button class="sc-btn" id="nb16b-run">Run &#119967; on (save idle)&#969;</button>
    <span style="font-size:0.85rem;color:var(--sc-label);">the general obstruction: delay each save past the next visit to <em>d</em><sub>0</sub></span>
  </div>
  <div class="sc-panel">
    <h4>Run of &#119967; (period shown 4&times;)</h4>
    <div class="run-strip" id="nb16b-strip"></div>
    <div id="nb16b-verdict"></div>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
(function(){
  const delta={d0:{save:'d1',edit:'d0',idle:'d0'},d1:{save:'d1',edit:'d0',idle:'d0'}};
  const F=new Set(['d0']);
  function run(){
    const v=['save','idle']; const seq=[].concat(...Array(4).fill(v));
    const strip=document.getElementById('nb16b-strip'), verdict=document.getElementById('nb16b-verdict');
    strip.innerHTML='';
    let state='d0'; const tail=new Set();
    seq.forEach((s,i)=>{
      state=delta[state][s]; tail.add(state);
      const box=document.createElement('span');
      box.className='tok'+(s==='save'?' save':'');
      box.innerHTML=`${s}<br><small style="font-weight:400">${state}${F.has(state)?' &#9733;':''}</small>`;
      strip.appendChild(box);
    });
    const good=[...tail].some(q=>F.has(q));
    verdict.innerHTML=`<div class="verdict-box verdict-fail"><strong>&#119967; accepts</strong> — d<sub>0</sub>&#8712;F is visited infinitely often (every <code>idle</code>). But the word has <strong>infinitely many saves</strong>, so a correct recogniser of "finitely many saves" must <strong>reject</strong> it. &#119967; is wrong — and every DBA fails the same way: after any finite prefix an all-<code>idle</code> continuation must be accepted, so the unique run must revisit an accepting state; delay the next save until after that visit, repeat forever, and you get infinitely many saves with infinitely many accepting visits.</div>`;
  }
  document.getElementById('nb16b-run').addEventListener('click',run);
  run();
})();
</script>
```

The lesson is **not** that complementation is impossible — $\omega$-regular languages *are* closed under complement. It is that the finite-word state-swapping shortcut does not transfer. The rest of the chapter builds the complement algebraically, via the congruence $\approx_{\mathcal A}$ and a Ramsey decomposition — see **[Notebook 21](21-approx-a-profile.qmd)** and **[Notebook 23](23-ramsey-decomposition.qmd)**.
